source.title: Deep networks for system identification: a Survey
source.authors: G. Pillonetto; A. Aravkin; D. Gedon; L. Ljung; Antônio H. Ribeiro; T. Schon

record.file_problem: The full survey text is present. Some equations and figure layouts are flattened, so plotted values cannot be recovered precisely.
record.tranche_reason: The survey reports its own generalization results in system identification, a new setting for the mapped width and overparameterization finding. Other relevant findings are discussed or cited rather than tested by the survey.
record.gate_note: The survey cites prior results on fitting random labels, convolutional architectures, optimizer comparisons, large batches, dropout, sharpness, and memorized examples; those cited results are not rows. Section 6.2's description of Neyshabur et al.'s width result is also cited prior work. The survey's own Figure 12 tests a related width/generalization question with random Fourier features in nonlinear ARX models. Its system identification validation examples report regression fit, not classification accuracy or random-label controls.
record.test_reason: The survey discusses the claim versions but its own experiments do not test them. R1 varies fixed random Fourier features in minimum-norm nonlinear ARX regression, rather than widening a neural network trained with gradient methods as V2 specifies. The remaining experiments measure system-identification performance without the comparisons required by V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors present deep networks and concatenated kernels as useful system-identification model structures, illustrate good generalization despite overparameterization, and discuss double descent alongside cases where interpolation is less robust than tuned regularization. They identify theory for dynamically generated data and robustness or uncertainty bounds as open problems.
record.recipe_differences: The survey synthesizes prior deep-learning methods and reports system-identification examples. Its width sweep uses random Fourier features in nonlinear ARX regression, not the mapped one-hidden-layer ReLU image-classification setup.
record.method_sensitivity: In the stable spline pseudo-inverse comparison, relative validation fit changes between low-pass and white Gaussian noise inputs (R2–R5).

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 12 describes test MSE falling again beyond interpolation as random-feature count increases; minimum-norm solutions are selected. Test MSE versus parameter norm instead has a U-shaped relationship.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm random-feature nonlinear ARX regression can exhibit double descent as feature count increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Tuned stable-spline regularization and minimum stable-spline norm interpolation perform comparably under low-pass validation inputs, while tuned regularization is more robust under white-noise validation inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative predictive performance of regularized and minimum-norm interpolating system estimators depends on validation input statistics.

fits_no_version.finding: The Silverbox example reports 99.18% validation fit for the deep cascadeforward model versus 29.71% for the Box-Jenkins model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A deep nonlinear ARX model can substantially outperform the reported linear Box-Jenkins baseline on Silverbox validation data.

fits_no_version.finding: FC, LSTM and deep state-space models with 111902–184210 parameters trained on 300 time samples perform well on held-out coupled-drive data relative to a linear ARX baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Highly overparameterized deep system-identification models can achieve good held-out regression performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Automatisierungstechnik (venue shown as “at - Automatisierungstechnik” in the supplied metadata)
record.problems: The main double-descent evidence in Fig. 12 is plotted without numerical values or stated uncertainty. The survey's own deep-model validation results concern dynamical-system regression, not classification. In several examples the figure provides boxplots but the text does not report exact fits.
record.rows_left_out: No cited prior-study results were included as rows. For Fig. 12, the exact train/test curve values are figure-only and are represented by one row for the test-error sweep rather than separate plotted points. The Fig. 14 and Fig. 20 boxplots are represented as separate model/condition rows where applicable, without reconstructing numeric values.

untested.parts: No experiment comparing random-label memorization with natural-label held-out classification performance using the same architecture and training recipe.
No width sweep of neural networks trained to convergence with gradient methods beyond zero training error. The cited Neyshabur result is prior work; Figure 12 instead varies fixed random features.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison or test of learned local connectivity.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison of held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
No batch-size experiment with controlled epoch budgets or adapted training recipes.
No held-out comparison with and without dropout.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization gaps against alternative measures.
No removal and retraining experiment comparing highly memorized examples with random removals.

record.verdict_notes: The post-interpolation decrease in Figure 12 is a related result, not evidence for V2's trained-network width claim. Neither this mismatch nor the absence of the other required experiments warrants a limits_scope verdict. Figure 12 is described as adapted from reference [278].

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label classification comparison; no CIFAR or ImageNet experiment.
The sweep uses random Fourier features in a nonlinear ARX model, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10. It does not test the mapped width-specific setting.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD held-out comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with other generalization measures.

rows.subject: Nonlinear ARX model with Random Fourier Features
rows.size_stated: Number of features m varied relative to N=100 training samples; m indicates number of features rather than model parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of random Fourier features and measured one-step-ahead training and test mean square error.

conditions.value: Nonlinear ARX data generated using the nonlinear function presented in [72], with v(t) ∼ N(0, 1).

rows.measure: One-step-ahead mean square error on test data as a function of m/N; training error also plotted.
rows.note: The text describes a double-descent test-error curve: error rises near interpolation and then falls as m/N increases beyond 1. Exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The double-descent pattern is explicitly described, but it does not establish V2 for trained neural networks. Features are fixed random Fourier features and only their output coefficients are estimated; minimum parameter norm selects among interpolating solutions. The result description is in Section 6.3, with experimental details in the Figure 12 caption, rather than Section 6.2.

rows.subject: ReLS-TC
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated prediction fit on a validation set after regularized least-squares estimation using stable spline/TC regularization.
rows.uncertainty: 100-run boxplots shown; exact spread figure only
rows.note: The prose says ReLS-TC gives the best results and PI-TC is comparable for this validation set; precise fits are only plotted.
rows.check: Comparison of regularized and interpolating system-identification estimators; no claim version is measured. Exact prediction fits are not recoverable from the supplied figure text.

rows.subject: PI-TC
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated prediction fit on a validation set using a minimum stable spline norm interpolating estimator.
rows.uncertainty: 100-run boxplots shown; exact spread figure only
rows.note: The prose characterizes PI-TC's prediction performance as comparable to ReLS-TC on this validation set.
rows.check: Comparable prediction fit to ReLS-TC does not constitute partial evidence for any version. This is an estimator comparison outside the claims.

rows.subject: ReLS-TC
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated prediction fit on a validation set after regularized least-squares estimation using stable spline/TC regularization.
rows.uncertainty: 100-run boxplots shown; exact spread figure only
rows.note: The prose says carefully tuned regularization may lead to more robust predictions under input variations than minimum-norm solutions.
rows.check: Greater robustness of tuned regularization under changed input statistics measures none of V1–V8; observed is not a claim-relative state here.

rows.uncertainty: 100-run boxplots shown; exact spread figure only

rows.subject: Box-Jenkins model (mbj)
rows.size_stated: 4 poles, 4 zeros, and a second-order noise transfer function
rows.operation_detail: Compared simulated output with validation data for the Silverbox benchmark.

rows.note: This is a regression validation result in system identification.

rows.subject: Deep cascadeforwardnet model (mN2)

rows.operation_detail: Compared simulated output with Silverbox validation data after estimating a nonlinear ARX model.
rows.measure: Fit, percent of output variation reproduced
rows.note: The prose describes the simulation as remarkably good; the validation data character is quite different from the estimation data.
rows.check: The prose reports 99.18% validation fit, but comparison with a Box-Jenkins model tests none of the versions. Flattened figure labels also contain 99.31%; retain 99.18% as the explicitly reported numerical result and flag the discrepancy.
